title: Kernel fallback & retry heuristics deep dive — Aurora Bio
summary: Deep dive on intermittent CUDA OOMs and kernel fallbacks observed during long-context gen. Focus on root causes: memory fragmentation, KV caching growth, quantization operator fallbacks, and retry semantics. Agreed repro plan, suggested config changes for batching/KV eviction, and next steps for shared logs and a controlled load run.
topics: KV cache growth and eviction policies
action_items: Samir Patel: Share internal kernel-fallback design doc and retry policy summary by 2026-03-18
Liam O'Connor: Upload full repro logs (driver, dmesg, runtime logs, batcher traces) to shared S3 by 2026-03-17
Jin Wu: Prepare a pared-down repro script (container + synthetic load) for Aurora to run on their on-prem cluster by 2026-03-20
Mariana Lopes: Run automated memory-defrag experiment on staging and report results by 2026-03-22
Hannah Schultz: Provide exact model config (max_seq, batcher settings, quantization flags) used in production by 2026-03-17
next_steps: Redwood to confirm recommended retry window and backoff defaults for Dedicated clusters
Aurora to run Redwood's repro container in their air-gapped environment and share pass/fail
Schedule follow-up to review staging defrag results and decide on default eviction policy
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-15
Start time: 14:30 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Jin (Redwood SE), Mariana (Redwood SRE), Dr. Priya Menon (Aurora Head of AI), Liam O'Connor (Aurora ML Infra), Hannah Schultz (Aurora Platform)

Automated summary (auto-generated, quick): intermittent CUDA OOMs during long-context generation; sometimes kernel fallback to CPU or a non-tensorcore kernel; retries cause duplicate partial outputs unless idempotency handled; KV cache growth suspected.

[00:00:07] Samir (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — we want to get to root cause of those production OOMs you saw on long-context jobs, walk through kernel fallback behavior, and agree a repro path and mitigations.

[00:00:22] Priya (Aurora): Yep, yep. Thanks. It has been pretty disruptive — we saw jobs that normally run fine start failing after 30–45 minutes, always during the same workload pattern, long prefix + dynamic prompt.

[00:00:36] Jin (Redwood): Quick question on your setup — are you on Dedicated nodes or Private on-prem? And driver versions?

[00:00:43] Liam (Aurora): We're on our on-prem cluster, essentially Redwood Private. Nodes are A40-ish class, NVIDIA driver 525.85, cuDNN 8.4. We pinned the runtime to r1.12 in January.

[00:00:55] Mariana (Redwood): Noted. Two immediate things that jump out — driver/RT mismatch can cause fallback to older kernels, and fragmentation can present as OOMs even when nominal memory is available. Also we saw your note that enabling 4-bit quant caused more instability.

[00:01:14] Hannah (Aurora): Yeah, the 4-bit quant - it's a big one. Sometimes the log says "kernel failed, falling back to reference implementation" and then latency spikes. Not always OOM, but sometimes the fallback path later triggers OOM under sustained load.

[00:01:30] Jin (Redwood): That's consistent with what we've seen in other customers: certain operators in 4-bit quantize paths don't have optimized tensorcore kernels for the exact shape; the runtime falls back to a generic kernel which is slower and uses more intermediate memory. The batching window keeps queuing requests and the combined memory spikes.

[00:01:49] Samir (Redwood): Can you walk us through one of the crash traces you uploaded? Liam, you shared a tarball (s3://redwood-shared/aurora/repro-0315.tar.gz) — has the dmesg and driver logs.

[00:01:58] Liam (Aurora): Yes, uploaded that. There's a crash at 14:12:33 UTC — I can paste a snippet.

[00:02:10] (brief screen-share / silence)

[00:02:22] Liam (Aurora): Log line: "CUDA error: out of memory when allocating 512MB (cudaMalloc)" followed by "kernel fallback: launching reference-generic kernel" and then later several NCCL warnings about peer-to-peer failing (we have multi-GPU in some racks).

[00:02:41] Jin (Redwood): NCCL warnings are important — if comms degrade, we sometimes see additional buffering pending on the host while NCCL retries, which increases host pinned memory pressure. Combined with kernel fallback and slower throughput, it can cascade into OOM.

[00:02:58] Priya (Aurora): We also noticed that restarting the batcher sometimes stabilizes things. If we clear the KV cache or restart the process the errors stop for a while.

[00:03:10] Mariana (Redwood): That implies the KV cache is growing or not being evicted promptly. Can you confirm your KV cache config — is it per-model or per-tenant?

[00:03:19] Hannah (Aurora): It's per-tenant, and we increased the max_kv_entries to avoid repeated recompute. We thought that would help latency but maybe it's causing memory pressure.

[00:03:30] Jin (Redwood): Right. Large KV caches are great for token cost, but they need eviction heuristics (LRU or time-based). Also look at headroom settings: the runtime has a memory headroom cap which, if set too low, will allow aggressive caching.

[00:03:45] Samir (Redwood): Quick digression — retry semantics. When the runtime triggers a kernel fallback and the request times out client-side, are you seeing retries from the client or from your frontend?

[00:03:55] Liam (Aurora): We have an upstream gateway that retries after 5s and again after 20s for certain error classes. We didn't qualify the idempotency fully — so we've had duplicate token streams once.

[00:04:07] Jin (Redwood): That explains duplicate partial outputs. Recommendation: treat fallback and transient CUDA errors as soft-fail with exponential backoff retry at the gateway layer and ensure idempotency keys per request. Also, Redwood runtime can surface error classes to help you make retry decisions (e.g., transient_device, kernel_fallback, oom_non_recoverable).

[00:04:28] Priya (Aurora): Is there any way to make the runtime avoid the fallback path entirely? We prefer predictable slow responses to unstable OOMs.

[00:04:36] Mariana (Redwood): Two approaches: 1) Prevent fallback by ensuring the optimized kernels exist — that means matching driver/cuDNN versions and enabling Redwood's kernel cache pre-warm step at startup. 2) Allow fallback but gate it: if a fallback occurs, throttle batching or evict KV entries for that model for a short cool-down window. That is a policy we can implement as a config on Dedicated/Private.

[00:05:01] Hannah (Aurora): Kernel cache pre-warm? We didn't run that.

[00:05:05] Jin (Redwood): It's a startup job that probes hot operator shapes and compiles or loads preferred kernels; it increases startup by a few seconds but avoids JIT-like compile/fallback during runtime. We'll share the script.

[00:05:16] (small cross-talk)

[00:05:30] Samir (Redwood): Let's talk batching. Your logs showed the batcher spike to 512 tokens queued and then many requests waited in the window. What is your soft latency SLO?

[00:05:39] Priya (Aurora): We aim for p95 < 250ms for short calls but for long-context gen we accept higher tail, up to 1.2s sometimes. But some of these jobs are interactive enough that spikes break front-end UX.

[00:05:51] Jin (Redwood): We recommend a soft batch window with a hard cap. Soft window of 50ms, hard flush at 200ms and a batch size cap of N (we'll recommend exact N by model and sequence length). Also enable per-origin queue limits so a single tenant can't inflate intermediate memory.

[00:06:10] Liam (Aurora): If we lower the batch cap, cost goes up though. Any advice balancing?

[00:06:16] Mariana (Redwood): Yes — tradeoff: lower batching reduces peak memory but increases token cost. Our Optimize toolkit can run an economic simulation on your throughput traces and recommend a configuration that meets your SLO while limiting memory headroom. We'll run that for you.

[00:06:31] Priya (Aurora): About quantization — any known failure modes with 4-bit on A40s?

[00:06:37] Jin (Redwood): A40's tensor core coverage is fine but some GEMM shapes used by the model when sequence length changes (esp. sliding windows for cross-attention) have no optimized int4 kernel in our current kernel set. Then runtime picks a slower float kernel and the memory pattern changes. Those infrequent shape changes are the Achilles' heel.

[00:06:55] Hannah (Aurora): Could we just force the runtime to use the float kernel always? Might be slower but more stable.

[00:07:01] Jin (Redwood): Yes — you can set "prefer_stable_kernels": true in the model profile. That avoids shape-specific int4 fast paths. We'll provide guidance on expected latency hit.

[00:07:12] Priya (Aurora): Driver versions — we are locked to 525.x for other infra compatibility. Will that be a hard blocker?

[00:07:19] Mariana (Redwood): Not necessarily a blocker but it limits available optimized kernels. We can backport some kernels to work with 525.x but that's extra engineering; part of our recommendation is to test pre-warm on a staging node with 525.x and see which kernels fall back. We'll supply the compatibility matrix.

[00:07:36] (notes being typed)

[00:07:44] Samir (Redwood): Let's get specific: reproduction. Jin, can you outline the minimal repro we want Aurora to run?

[00:07:52] Jin (Redwood): Sure. 1) Use our repro container (we'll share image tag) that runs a loop of long-prefix generation with max_seq=8192 and intermittent shorter sequences to exercise shape changes. 2) Set KV cache to the same per-tenant size you use. 3) Run under your normal batcher settings for 30–60 minutes while collecting cuda-smi, dmesg, runtime logs, and batcher traces. We'll provide example commands and the container.

[00:08:17] Liam (Aurora): We'll try that in our air-gapped cluster. Any special kernel modules or driver flags?

[00:08:24] Jin (Redwood): We recommend enabling "allow_pinned_host_memory": true, and collect pcie errors; but do not change allocation behavior — we want to reproduce as-is. Also enable our verbose backend logging for a short window.

[00:08:36] Priya (Aurora): One more thing — we observed that when a worker OOMs the orchestrator restarts it and sometimes it recovers but other times it triggers a flurry of container restarts across other pods. Is there a recommended restart policy?

[00:08:48] Mariana (Redwood): For K8s on-prem, use a backoff restart policy: initialDelay 10s, max backoff 5m, and use readiness probes that keep traffic away from a worker until pre-warm completes. Also limit the number of restarts per minute to avoid stampeding.

[00:09:05] Hannah (Aurora): Good. We'll adopt that.

[00:09:12] Jin (Redwood): A note on idempotency keys again — whichever retry policy you pick, ensure clients send an idempotency token. Our SDK supports dedup; if we see retry duplicates we can collapse them server-side when idempotency present.

[00:09:28] (short pause)

[00:09:35] Samir (Redwood): Ok — high-level recommended mitigations: 1) run kernel pre-warm on staging and compare fallback rate, 2) adjust batcher soft/hard windows and per-tenant queue caps, 3) add KV eviction LRU/time-based policy and memory headroom caps, 4) set retry semantics at the gateway with exponential backoff + idempotency, 5) if needed prefer stable kernels over int4 fast paths.

[00:09:58] Priya (Aurora): Sounds actionable. Can you put those in an internal doc and send?

[00:10:05] Samir (Redwood): Yes — we'll share a concise mitigation doc and the repro container. Action items as noted.

[00:10:12] (longer section — technical Q&A, jittery transcription)

[00:22:05] Liam (Aurora): Quick micro-question — we sometimes see "cudaLaunchKernel failed: unspecified launch failure" followed by a short spike and then OOM. Any pointer?

[00:22:15] Jin (Redwood): Unspecified launch failures are often symptomatic: preceding the error, operator did an allocation and returned an error but the runtime reported the subsequent kernel as failed. Check for asynchronous error reporting semantics; ensure you call cudaDeviceSynchronize in the repro harness to surface earlier errors.

[00:22:39] Priya (Aurora): We'll add synchronization points to catch the first error.

[00:34:50] Hannah (Aurora): Another intermittent detail: sometimes the fallback happens only on GPU-0 and not on GPU-1 on the same node. Is that expected?

[00:35:02] Mariana (Redwood): Could be thermal/driver-level difference or a pinned allocation fragmentation on GPU-0. Also check BIOS/firmware and ECC settings — sometimes they affect memory alignment and allocator behavior.

[00:46:00] Samir (Redwood): Wrapping up — agreed next steps are the ones in Action Items. We'll set up a follow-up in a week to review initial repro results. Thanks everyone.

Meeting end.
